question: When we talk about the maternal mortality ratio, what exactly are we measuring?

options.A: Deaths of mothers per 100,000 live births
options.B: Total number of pregnant women in a country
options.C: Number of complicated deliveries per hospital
options.D: Deaths of infants under one year of age

explanation: You've got this! The maternal mortality ratio is simply the number of maternal deaths for every 100,000 live births. It helps us track and improve safety for mothers. [learn more](GNS226_U1_T014#GNS226_U1_T014_h1)

question: Why do public health experts say that most maternal deaths are preventable?

options.A: Because traditional herbs can cure all pregnancy issues
options.B: Because pregnant women rarely develop severe complications
options.C: Because pregnancy complications always give weeks of warning
options.D: Because effective medical treatments and interventions exist

explanation: Spot on! With good antenatal care, skilled birth attendants, and quick emergency care, we can successfully manage and stop most life-threatening complications. [learn more](GNS226_U1_T014#GNS226_U1_T014_h1)

question: What makes postpartum hemorrhage (PPH) such a major emergency for a new mother?

options.A: Chronic infection of the urinary tract
options.B: Severe blood loss that can quickly cause death
options.C: Permanent paralysis of the lower limbs

explanation: Exactly. Postpartum hemorrhage means rapid, heavy bleeding after birth. If we don't replace the blood volume quickly, it can lead to severe shock and danger very fast. [learn more](GNS226_U1_T014#GNS226_U1_T014_h2)

question: A pregnant patient comes in with a pounding headache, changes in her vision, and very high blood pressure. What is the most likely condition?
explanation: Well done! High blood pressure paired with headaches and visual changes are classic warning signs of preeclampsia that every nurse needs to watch out for. [learn more](GNS226_U1_T014#GNS226_U1_T014_h2)

question: When does puerperal sepsis typically show up in a patient?
explanation: You got it! Puerperal sepsis is a reproductive tract infection that develops after childbirth or a miscarriage, up to 42 days into the postpartum period. [learn more](GNS226_U1_T014#GNS226_U1_T014_h3)

question: Which of these is a common physical danger resulting from an unsafe abortion?
explanation: Correct! When procedures are done without proper training or sterile tools, it can easily tear the uterus and cause severe, life-threatening pelvic infections. [learn more](GNS226_U1_T014#GNS226_U1_T014_h3)

question: How do we tell an indirect obstetric cause of maternal death apart from a direct one?

options.A: It has no relation to the female reproductive system at all
options.B: It only happens during the third trimester of labor
options.C: It is exclusively caused by surgical errors
options.D: It is caused by a pre-existing medical condition worsened by pregnancy

explanation: Spot on! Indirect causes are medical issues like heart disease or severe malaria that were already there, but got dangerously worse because of the physical changes of pregnancy. [learn more](GNS226_U1_T014#GNS226_U1_T014_h4)

question: Why is severe anemia especially dangerous for a woman going into labor?

options.A: She has very little reserve to survive normal blood loss during delivery
options.B: She will automatically develop eclampsia within hours
options.C: Her contractions will completely stop during the first stage
options.D: Her baby will be born with severe bone deformities

explanation: You're doing great! Every delivery involves some blood loss. A mom with low blood levels (anemia) cannot afford even a small loss without sliding into shock. [learn more](GNS226_U1_T014#GNS226_U1_T014_h4)

question: In the famous 'Three Delays' model, what is the first delay all about?

options.A: The wait time to see a doctor at the hospital
options.B: The time spent traveling on bad rural roads
options.C: The decision by the family to seek medical help
options.D: The delay in manufacturing lifesaving drugs

explanation: Exactly right! The first delay happens right at home when family members take too long to recognize danger signs or decide it's time to visit a clinic. [learn more](GNS226_U1_T014#GNS226_U1_T014_h5)

question: A woman in labor in a remote village has a uterine rupture, but the family cannot find a vehicle to take her to the hospital. Which delay does this represent?

options.A: Delay in diagnosing the initial pregnancy
options.B: Delay in receiving adequate treatment at the hospital
options.C: Delay in deciding to seek care
options.D: Delay in reaching a medical facility

explanation: You nailed it. Distance, bad roads, and transport troubles fall squarely under the second delay—getting from home to a health facility. [learn more](GNS226_U1_T014#GNS226_U1_T014_h5)

question: Which factor is consistently linked with pregnant women making better use of antenatal care?

options.B: Living in a densely populated urban slum
options.C: Strict adherence to traditional childbirth herbs
options.D: Having a large extended family at home

explanation: Spot on! Educated women are usually more aware of health risks, understand advice better, and feel more confident seeking professional care early. [learn more](GNS226_U1_T014#GNS226_U1_T014_h6)

question: How can gender inequality play an indirect role in maternal mortality?

options.A: By altering the chromosomal makeup of the developing fetus
options.B: By speeding up the natural labor process to unsafe levels
options.C: By directly causing sudden postpartum hemorrhage after delivery
options.D: By depriving women of decision-making power over their own health and finances

explanation: That's correct. When women lack a voice in household decisions or money, they might struggle to get timely permission or funds to go to the clinic during an emergency. [learn more](GNS226_U1_T014#GNS226_U1_T014_h6)

question: Which of the following is a classic danger sign in pregnancy that a patient must report immediately?
explanation: You got it! Vaginal bleeding at any point in pregnancy is never normal—it can point to serious issues like placenta previa and needs quick medical attention. [learn more](GNS226_U1_T014#GNS226_U1_T014_h7)

question: As a nurse, what is your main goal when doing a risk assessment during antenatal care?

options.A: To accurately predict the exact day and hour of delivery
options.B: To eliminate the need for any laboratory blood tests
options.C: To detect potential complications early before they become life-threatening
options.D: To diagnose all genetic disorders in the unborn infant

explanation: Brilliant! Screening lets us spot moms who need extra support or specialized care early on, keeping both mother and baby safe. [learn more](GNS226_U1_T014#GNS226_U1_T014_h7)

question: What is the primary goal of family planning when it comes to maternal health?

options.A: To replace the need for routine antenatal checkups
options.B: To increase the total birth rate in rural areas
options.C: To space pregnancies and prevent high-risk births
options.D: To completely eradicate all infectious diseases

explanation: Spot on! Family planning gives women control over their pregnancies, helping them avoid very young or older high-risk ages and keeping healthy gaps between kids. [learn more](GNS226_U1_T014#GNS226_U1_T014_h8)

question: Why is the active management of the third stage of labor so important in nursing practice?

options.A: It speeds up the dilation of the cervix
options.B: It prevents preeclampsia from developing postpartum
options.C: It guarantees that the baby will not have jaundice
options.D: It helps prevent excessive postpartum bleeding

explanation: You nailed the final one! Using uterotonics and careful cord traction right after baby arrives is key to keeping postpartum hemorrhage at bay. Great job! [learn more](GNS226_U1_T014#GNS226_U1_T014_h8)
